title: Tav Prasad Savaiye
hookLine: ten verses saying that kings, armies and rituals are nothing without love
last: JAAP SAHIB — THE RHYTHM OF PRAISE.

cards: Scroll any feed for five minutes and you'll see what the world calls impressive. The mansion. The supercar.
The influencer at a holy site at sunrise, perfectly lit. Followers in the millions.

Centuries ago a poet saw the equivalent of all that in his own day, the richest kings, the biggest armies, the most admired ascetics and pilgrims, and he wrote ten short poems that keep turning back to one thought.
All of it, he says, is worth nothing, without one thing.

teach.b: The poems are the Tav Prasad Savaiye, the third bani of the Sikh morning. Tav prasad means by your grace. Savaiya is the poetic form: a four-line verse with long, flowing lines, beautiful to recite.
These ten come from Guru Gobind Singh's Akal Ustat, the praise of the Timeless, in the Dasam Granth.

teach.h: A PARADE OF KINGS AND HOLY MEN.
teach.b: Each verse is a parade. In paraphrase: I have seen the pure ascetics, the yogis, the celibates, crowds of them.
I have seen mighty kings riding elephants with golden trappings, great horses, armies without number, emperors who conquered the earth.
I have seen pilgrims bathing at every holy river, people fasting, people performing every ritual. Then, as the verses close, the turn: without the Lord, without love, none of it counts for anything.

teach.h: ONLY THOSE WHO LOVED FOUND GOD.
teach.b: And the well-known line, again in paraphrase: I tell the truth, listen, everyone: only those who loved found the Lord. Notice who is saying this.

teach.h: A LEADER OF ARMIES SAYS IT.
teach.b: Guru Gobind Singh was himself a leader of armies, who knew horses and weapons and power from the inside. He's not sneering at kings from the outside. From someone who knew that world, the savaiyas say: it isn't the thing.
Neither, they say, is outward religion done without love. They're gentle with no one's pride, including the pride of the pious. What remains after the parade passes?
Love. That's why these ten verses sit in the morning. Before the day starts measuring you by what you own or how you look, the savaiyas measure differently.

how: The ten Tav Prasad Savaiye, from Guru Gobind Singh's Akal Ustat, are recited every morning in Nitnem after Jaap Sahib, and are among the five banis of the Amrit ceremony.

o: a prayer said while bowing to the floor
a short chorus repeated between hymns
a four-line verse of long, flowing lines

games.q: what's inside the savaiyas — tap the pairs.
p: a four-line verse of long lines
where the ten savaiyas come from
only those who loved found God

s: the savaiyas praise great kings and armies
they parade them past and say none of it counts without love.
Guru Gobind Singh, who wrote them, led armies himself
he speaks as someone who knew power from the inside.
the savaiyas only criticize worldly people
they're equally sharp about outward religion done for show.

games.q: the parade has passed: kings, elephants, yogis, pilgrims at every river. what do the savaiyas say finds the Lord?
games.why: I tell the truth, listen, everyone: only those who loved found the Lord.

practice: If you can, play a recording of Tav Prasad Savaiye and listen to just the first verse, about a minute, noticing the long, rolling lines.
If you can't, hold one thing you've been proud of lately, a promotion, a purchase, a good photo, and ask the savaiyas' question: was there love in it? No judgment, just the question.

wordCard.voice: Savaiya. A four-line verse with long, flowing lines. Guru Gobind Singh's ten savaiyas keep returning to one thought: without love, nothing.
